action: Tell developers to enter device codes only for sign-ins they started, review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations, and set Copilot CLI cloud session storage and memory to the least permissive setting that works.
exec: AI coding agents widen what a phished sign-in can reach, including code, past sessions and local commands; restrict agent session and memory settings.
plain: Microsoft tested how tricking a developer into typing a sign-in code could let a hacker control their AI coding assistant and read their private code. It has not seen this used in real attacks yet.

key_findings: In a controlled simulation, a test account approved a GitHub device-code request started by an attacker-controlled client using the public Copilot CLI client ID.
With that approval researchers could steer a remote-control-enabled Copilot CLI session to run a command, add misleading memory entries, read synced sessions and access private repositories.
The requested scopes included repo, read:user, read:org, gist and codespace, chosen by the client that starts the flow.
The technique applies to any public client supporting the device flow; Microsoft has not observed these four outcomes in the wild.
Microsoft cites earlier device-code phishing campaigns including Storm-2372 and EvilTokens, which it helped disrupt in September 2026.
recommendations: Approve device codes only for sign-ins you started yourself, even on the genuine github.com page.
Review GitHub Copilot CLI session storage and remote-control policy and choose the least permissive setting.
Review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations and limit repository access by role.
Review Copilot Memory for suspicious entries, and connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps for visibility.

summary: Microsoft researchers showed in a lab that a phished GitHub device-code approval for the Copilot CLI client could let an attacker steer a remotely controllable agent session, plant misleading memory entries, read cloud-synced sessions and reach private repositories. These are proof-of-concept results, not attacks seen in the wild. Microsoft added two Defender XDR detections for the email and Teams lures.
title: Microsoft: one phished device-code approval could let attackers steer AI coding agents

validation.note: Reviewed against the full original Microsoft Security Blog post; lab proof of concept only.

review.note: Four lab outcomes, not-in-the-wild statement and two Defender XDR detections match the Microsoft blog post.
